explain.say: Earth is closer to the Sun and moves faster on a shorter track. About every 26 months, Earth catches up with Mars and overtakes it, like a car passing a slower one on the inside lane.

faq.a: Planets closer to the Sun orbit faster and have shorter paths. Earth takes one year to go round; Mars takes about 1.9 years, so Earth catches up and passes it about every 26 months.
asks: How often does Earth pass Mars?

faq.a: It is when a planet seems to move backwards, westward, against the stars for a while. It happens when Earth overtakes an outer planet, or an inner planet overtakes Earth; no planet really reverses.
Around the time Earth overtakes it, called opposition, when Mars is closest to us and opposite the Sun in the sky. That is right in the middle of its backward loop.

faq.q: Do other planets go backwards too?
faq.a: Yes. All the planets appear to go backwards at times. Outer planets like Jupiter and Saturn do it when Earth passes them, and Mercury and Venus when they overtake Earth.

faq.q: How did ancient astronomers explain the loops?
faq.a: Ptolemy's Earth-centred model added small circles called epicycles to make planets loop. Copernicus showed in 1543 that a Sun-centred system explains the loops naturally, as Earth overtaking slower outer planets.

facts: Earth overtakes Mars about every 26 months, when Mars reaches opposition.
Mars takes about 687 Earth days to orbit the Sun.
Nicolaus Copernicus published his Sun-centred model in 1543.
